CMC landed on this list last year due to calf concerns carried over from 2024. He responded by playing every game and finishing as the overall RB1. The fantasy community is once again pointing to his injury history and offseason coachspeak about managing his snap count, but CMC still would have led all running backs in fantasy points last season with five to ten percent fewer snaps. He ranks behind only Bijan Robinson and Jahmyr Gibbs in Walter’s running back projections, and has finished top-2 among running backs ...

Barkley struggled in 2025. He went from leading the NFL in rushes over 20 yards to recording just one, while his touchdown rate dropped from 3.8% to 2.5% despite averaging approximately one carry per game inside the five-yard line. A new offensive coordinator should improve the Eagles’ rushing efficiency, and Barkley projects to rank top-5 in touches per game for a fifth consecutive season. He is a strong late first or early second-round pick at his current ADP.

It was a tale of two seasons in 2025. Four straight games of 15 or more fantasy points to open the year, followed by just two games over 15 points in his next eight before a season-ending injury. The core concern remains his catch rate: 52.5% as a rookie in 2024, then an abysmal 48.9% (WR118) in 2025. A league-average catch rate would unlock top-15 fantasy wide receiver upside.

McLaurin ranked ninth among receivers in yards per route run in 2025, which was the second best mark of his career. He scored just three touchdowns while missing seven games and playing part of the season without **Jayden Daniels**. The frustration from fantasy managers is understandable, but a healthy Daniels and a new offensive coordinator in **David Blough**, who has stated the offense will be built around getting McLaurin ten targets per game, creates a legitimate top-12 wide receiver ceiling.

Worthy suffered a shoulder injury 3 snaps into Week 1 last season, and at the time many feared it would be a season-ending injury. He ended up missing just two games and playing through the injury the rest of a disappointing season. The Chiefs did very little to add to the receiver room this offseason, and Worthy’s disappointment last season is more than baked into his current draft cost, making him an interesting late-round dart throw.

To start the 2024 NFL season, Chris Godwin rattled off 7 straight games with at least 11.6 PPR fantasy points and was averaging 19.7 points per game (2nd best among wide receivers). Then, he suffered a significant ankle/leg injury that caused him to miss the rest of the season and the first 3 weeks of the 2025 season. In his 2nd game back last year, he suffered a Fibula injury that knocked him out 5 more weeks. When he eventually returned, Godwin averaged 13.4 PPR points per game from Week 13 to 17. Godwin’s draft ...

Reed suffered a broken collarbone in Week 2, causing him to miss the vast majority of the season. He had his first and only game with over a 65% snap share in the NFL playoffs. His injury-riddled 2025 season is suppressing his draft cost this year despite the fact that he’s 100% healthy heading into this season and his role could increase with the Packers no longer having Dontayvion Wicks or Romeo Doubs. ---

Barring injury to **Matthew Stafford**, Simpson offers zero fantasy value this season, and potentially next season as well. He was drafted in the 1st round to sit and learn. Put a tab on him and **check back in 2027.**

If the Cardinals are eliminated from playoff contention, there is a reasonable chance Beck takes over the starting job to close out the year. He was the most experienced quarterback in this class but offers no rushing ability. His fantasy ceiling as a starter is low.

Price lands in an ideal situation. **Zach Charbonnet** is recovering from an ACL tear suffered in the Divisional Round, making Price the likely Week 1 starter in Seattle. He possesses a strong goal line skill set but has serious question marks as a pass-catcher. His ADP will likely only climb between now and draft day and he will go in the middle rounds of fantasy drafts. He’s an interesting Zero-RB target but his ceiling will be capped in a committee role once Charbonnet returns.

**Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears** ahead of him on the depth chart limit Singleton’s redraft value. He will not be drafted in most leagues, but his diverse skill set fits **Brian Daboll’s** offense well. Monitor him as a potential waiver wire target if opportunity opens up.

Sadiq will not be a consistent fantasy producer as a rookie, but the Jets invested 1st round capital in him and Walter has him ranked inside the top-10 at the position with a ceiling of TE4. He ran the fastest 40-yard dash of any tight end in NFL history. His athleticism alone gives him a high ceiling trajectory. Monitor his target share early in the season.

Etienne is my favorite running back selection in this range of drafts. He has never had off-the-charts efficiency, but he is in line for a large workload in one of the faster-pace offenses in the NFL. He has a strong receiving and touchdown ceiling.

Javonte possesses massive TD upside. He scored 13 total touchdowns in 2025, and the Cowboys did not bring in any competition. His ADP is fair, and he’s on what expects to be one of the best offenses in the NFL.

Swift has been a top-25 RB in fantasy points per game every season of his career (six straight seasons). He’s a lock for 30+ receptions and is a great value at his current cost. Monangai is also a very underrated RB that offers lots of TD upside in his second season in Ben Johnson’s offense. If D’Andre Swift were to miss time, **Kyle Monangai** would have an elite league-winning ceiling. He’s a great pick a couple rounds later in your draft, especially in half-PPR and non-PPR leagues.

The second-year Jaguars RB is one of the few running backs with true league-winning upside in the early to mid rounds of drafts this year. Tuten should have significant volume on a top-tier offense and is the highest upside option in this backfield thanks to his superior big-play ability and receiving upside. **See the sleepers section for some of my favorite running back targets after round 6 of drafts.**

**Collins** averaged 16.2 fantasy points per game last season if you only look at games where he played 70%+ of snaps (removing all of his injury-impacted games). Over the last three seasons, Nico Collins ranks top-5 in yards per route run - he’s one of the most efficient receivers in the NFL. His floor and ceiling are well-established, and weekly top-3 upside at his current ADP makes him a strong pick.

**London** has increased his fantasy points per game every season since his rookie year, finishing with 16.7 points per game last season (WR8). Whether it’s **Tua Tagoviola** or Michael Penix, London should be near the top of the league in target share again this season making him a high floor and ceiling pick in round 2.

**Brown** has ranked top-12 in wide receiver fantasy points per game and top-10 in target share in four straight seasons, and there is no reason to expect that trend to stop with him on the Patriots. Brown has a top-5 ceiling in our projections now that he is catching passes from Drake Maye who led the NFL in yards per attempt last year.

Over the last three years, **Devonta Smith** has averaged 18.1 PPR points per game across his 26 games with at least 7 targets. That should be the norm for him this season with A.J. Brown no longer on the Eagles. Don’t let his small size fool you, he’s an excellent pick in round 3.

**Tee Higgins** averaged 19.3 fantasy points per game in 2024 (WR3), and 13.8 points per game in 2025 (WR15). His floor and ceiling are well-established, and weekly top-3 upside at his current ADP makes him a strong pick. He profiles similarly to George Pickens but at a one round discount in drafts.

**Ladd McConkey** finished as the WR37 in PPR points per game in 2025 despite three top-7 finishes between Weeks 6 and 10. Outside of that stretch, his production was pedestrian. With an improved offensive line, and Mike McDaniel calling the plays, Walter and I are anticipating a season similar to his rookie campaign.

**Luther Burden** had just two top-10 fantasy finishes as a rookie, but one came in Week 17, the fantasy championship. With D.J. Moore gone, Walter projects a sophomore jump for Burden as the clear target leader in Chicago. I’ll be chasing his ceiling in Round 5 every single time. Burden picked up a groin injury that will cause him to miss the entire pre-season, but reports suggest he is likely to be ready for Week 1. There is some added risk here, but this news has also dropped his cost in drafts by 1+ round acros...

**Terry McLaurin** missed seven games in 2025 and played much of the season without Jayden Daniels, a combination that made a strong fantasy finish impossible. Even with **Stefon Diggs** on the team, McLaurin is the clear top target on a team that projects to frequently play from behind. Our projections have McLaurin with an extremely safe floor (WR32) and an underrated ceiling (WR7), making him a strong value pick in the back half of Round 4 and beginning of Round 5.

**Emeka Egbuka** posted four top-12 fantasy finishes through his first nine games, including three top-4 finishes. His production hit a wall after that, with a WR38 in Week 15 being his best finish down the stretch. With Mike Evans gone, Egbuka’s role figures to be more consistent in year two and we’ve already seen proof of his elite ceiling. Second-year wide receivers have an impressive historical hit rate, making Egbuka a worthwhile pick in round 4.

2024 and 2025 saw consistent production from **Jameson Williams**, something that he didn’t have in his first two seasons. In 2025, Jamo went on an epic run between Weeks 6 and 15, scoring 16 or more PPR points seven times. Williams is capable of a WR1 finish on any given week. If that consistency carries into 2026, a top fantasy WR finish is well within reach. And you can get him in Round 5? I am so in.

**Christian Watson** has never had slimmer target competition, and his ceiling is well-established. He had four top-12 finishes, including three top-6 finishes in just ten regular season games in 2025. His touchdown upside paired with an expanded target share make him a strong value in Round 5.
**Washington** had five games with 17 or more PPR points from Week 9 on. It’s clear he will be a crucial weapon for the Jags moving forward with an excellent weekly floor in PPR leagues.

**Reed** missed most of last season due to a broken collarbone in Week 2, his only game playing more than 65% of snaps came in the NFL playoffs and he made the most of it, turning 7 targets into 15.7 PPR fantasy points. In 2024, Reed averaged 14.9 points per game in his 8 games over a 65% snap share. It’s very possible we see a weekly snap share over 65% with Doubs and Wicks no longer on the team, making Reed a worthwhile dart throw at this point of drafts if you are in need of a wide receiver.

**Downs** finds himself in a similar situation to Jayden Reed, albeit with a much worse quarterback situation. Over the last 2 years, Downs has averaged 14.5 PPR points per game in his 10 games playing at least 65% of the snaps. With **Michael Pittman** now on the Steelers and Alec Pierce likely to be sidelined most of training camp with an injury, it’s very likely we see a big jump in playing time for Josh Downs.

As mentioned in the injury bias section of the draft guide, Godwin’s fully healthy heading into this season (unlike last year) but his past injuries are making him extremely affordable in drafts. Over the last two years Godwin has averaged 15 fantasy points per game in his 14 games with at least a 65% snap share. He has a great chance to see a significant role with Mike Evans no longer on the team.

**Pittman Jr.** heads to Pittsburgh, not known for the passing attack over the past few years, but they have quietly made major upgrades to work alongside Metcalf like Pittman Jr. who will be the main target on intermediate routes. In all but one season since his rookie year, Pittman has been above 12 fantasy points per game, making him a major value as a bench WR in round 7+.

**Brock Bowers** followed the greatest rookie tight end fantasy season of all time with an injury-riddled second season, but his arrow is pointing up. He projects as the Raiders’ lead receiver with Kirk Cousins and Fernando Mendoza being a clear upgrade over Geno Smith. Bowers projects as the overall TE1 in our projections and his ceiling is breaking the single-season TE records with new head coach Klint Kubiak who showed last year he can get the most out of his team’s top receiver (with Jaxson Smith Njigba). The c...

**Loveland** is my favorite tight end pick this year because of his cost being substantially cheaper compared to Bowers and McBride. He has a path to matching McBride and Bowers on a per-game basis, Loveland rattled off three games over 21 fantasy points in his final 4 games last year including the NFL playoffs. In games where he played over 80% of snaps, he averaged 18.8 fantasy points per game, which would have ranked as the TE1 last season. Loveland is closer to the McBride/Bowers tier than the tier of tight end...

Last season Kraft finished top-10 four times out of his six games where he played 50% or more of the snaps, including two TE1 finishes. He was dominant before his injury, and target competition has only thinned since. Kraft has now ranked #1 among tight ends in yards per reception in back-to-back seasons, his league-winning upside is real.

**Kittle** profiles as an intriguing late-round value even though his Week 1 timeline is uncertain as he recovers from a torn achilles. He finished as the TE2 in PPR points per game and TE5 in target share in 2025. His fantasy production history speaks for itself. His injury is more than baked into his draft cost, making him a low risk high reward target in this range of drafts, especially if you draft a 2nd tight end to your team later. Once fully healthy, he can be a top-5 tight end in fantasy football.

**Andrews** posted an 11% touchdown rate in 2025, which was a step back from his 19.6% mark in 2024, but still among the best in the league at the position. He is in line for a larger role with Isaiah Likely now on the Giants yet his cost in drafts does not reflect that. Andrews should be a favorite target of **Lamar Jackson** and is available in round 9+ of most fantasy drafts. If you go with the late-round tight end strategy this season, Andrews is a great option with a top-10 TE ceiling to pair alongside a 2nd l...

Through the first three games of last season, Jackson was averaging an elite 27.6 fantasy points per game before suffering a hamstring injury in Week 4. He then averaged just 15.3 points per game in his 7 full games after he returned from the injury. Jackson is statistically the greatest rushing quarterback of all time, we saw his floor outcome last season but we don’t want to forget his league-winning ceiling. Coming off a disappointing year, Lamar has the potential to slide into round 5+ in some drafts.

**Maye** was the most efficient quarterback in the NFL last year, even when you adjust for strength of opponent. Now he enters year 3 with Romeo Doubs and A.J. Brown added to the roster. His elite floor and ceiling justify a 5th round pick this season.

**Daniels** had one of the greatest rookie fantasy seasons of all time in 2024, finishing with 22.4 fantasy points per game (QB4) and leading all quarterbacks with 54 rushing yards per game. He then played just 4 full games last season due to knee, hamstring, and elbow injuries. His ceiling makes him a high-value upside pick in this range of drafts, especially considering the potential boost from new offensive coordinator David Blough.

There are going to be drafts where **Jalen Hurts** falls into round 7+ because of the negative public sentiment surrounding him from last season and the departure of A.J. Brown. Yet, the tush-push remains a fantasy football cheat-code, especially in leagues with only 4 points per passing touchdown. Jalen Hurts has ranked top-10 in quarterback fantasy football points per game for 5-consecutive seasons, and he should benefit from having a new offensive coordinator after dealing with one of the worst coordinators in t...

Caleb jumped from 6.4 yards per attempt and a 3.6% touchdown rate in his rookie season to 7 yards per attempt and a 4.7% touchdown rate in his first season with head coach Ben Johnson. Our current projections are assuming similar efficiency to last season, and Williams still projects as a good value pick in round 7 of fantasy drafts. In year 2 of the Ben Johnson offense with Luther Burden and Colston Loveland also entering year 2, we should not be surprised if Caleb Williams efficiency takes another leap, giving hi...

Herbert averaged over 22.5 fantasy points per game in each of his first two seasons in the NFL (2020 and 2021) but has been under 19 points per game each of the last 4 seasons. We’ve already seen a Mike McDaniels offense lead the NFL in passing yards with Tua, so it would not be a surprise to see Herbert achieve that this season. He has the 4th highest ceiling in our projections, making him one of the ideal mid-round QB targets.

Following the Jakobi Meyers trade last season, Lawrence averaged an elite 25.7 fantasy points per game from Week 12 onwards. He finished the season with 8-consecutive games with at least 19 fantasy points. With one of the best wide receiver groups in the NFL, there is real overall QB1 upside here.

Purdy has quietly finished top-10 among quarterbacks in fantasy points per game in all 3 straight seasons. In his 8 full games (excluding Week 18) due to a shoulder and toe injury suffered early in the season he averaged 22.6 fantasy points per game last year, ranking 2nd best among quarterbacks behind only Josh Allen. With Mike Evans now on the team, the 49ers have arguably the best group of pass catchers in the NFL if George Kittle, CMC, and Deebo Samuel can stay healthy.

The Chargers open against the Cardinals and Raiders in Weeks 1 and 2, two of the softest matchups in the league. Their defense is one of the most underrated units in the NFL, and Walter has them ranked as the DEF7 with a ceiling of DEF1. After those matchups, the Chargers face a difficult stretch heading into their Week 7 bye, taking on the Bills, Seahawks, Broncos, and Chiefs. Stream them with confidence in the first two weeks, then look elsewhere until Week 16 when they play the Dolphins.

The Jaguars open against the Browns, a team with bottom-tier quarterback play breaking in an entirely new offensive system. Walter projects Jacksonville as the DEF12 in the Rest-of-Season Rankings, despite a difficult season-long schedule. They are a strong Week 1 streaming option.

Outside of Buffalo in Week 2, the Lions take on the Saints, Jets, Panthers, and Cardinals before their Week 6 bye. They have a much more daunting schedule after that, but they will be a formidable option early in the season in matchups with weak offenses.

Reichard is attached to a Vikings offense that was mediocre in 2025 but should improve in 2026. He made the fifth most field goals in the league last year on the eighth most attempts and was one of the most accurate kickers in football, hitting 94.3% of his tries, third-best among qualified kickers. Pair that volume with that accuracy and a dome to kick in, and you’ve got a guy with top three upside. Reichard is Walter’s K6 with a ceiling of K1.

Smyth, a Northern Ireland native, took over the Saints’ job late in the year and immediately looked the part, averaging 10.0 fantasy points per game, tied for fifth-best at the position. New Orleans attempted the third most field goals in the league last season, and Smyth gets the benefit of playing half his games in the Caesars Superdome. He’s tied to an ascending offense that should keep creating opportunities. Smyth is Walter’s K4 with a ceiling of K1.

“Steady” Eddy Pineiro doesn’t have flashy volume (it’s similar to Minnesota’s), but he’s in the most stable situation of the three. San Francisco’s offense is good, ranking top ten in both yards and points. Among kickers who started at least 14 games, Pineiro ranked fifth in points per game. Attach yourself to a good offense inside a tough division full of strong defenses, and there’s going to be a steady stream of high-leverage field goals. “Steady” Eddy makes them. Pineiro is Walter’s K7 with a ceiling of K1. ---

Jacobs ended last season with 3-straight games under 7 PPR fantasy points if we include the NFL playoffs, and he averaged just 8.7 points per game from Week 11-17. With **Marshawn Lloyd** looking fully healthy, it’s also likely we see a dip in usage and playing time for Jacobs this season. And I haven’t even mentioned the fact that Jacobs comes ...

**Todd Monken** has historically used a running back by committee approach, and while **Judkins** is a talented runner that likely means **Dylan Sampson** is the primary pass catcher in the backfield. Judkins averaged under 2 receptions per game last season, making him a TD dependent running back on an offense that could struggle to score points with one of the shakiest QB situations in the NFL.

What happens when **Zach Charbonnet** comes back for fantasy playoffs? I am also worried the Seahawks will be a committee without Charb. Also, there is no statistical evidence **Jadarian Price** can contribute as a pass-catcher. A touchdown-dependent committee back with a weaker playoff projection is a hard fade. TD-dependent committee back with a worse projection for the fantasy playoffs? Count me OUT.

In the first four weeks of the last season, **Tony Pollard** was in a true workhorse role, playing 86% of snaps with Tyjae Spears sidelined due to injury. After Spears returned, his snapshare fell to 53% the rest of the season. Pollard was unstartable for most of last season, he did not have a single game over 15 PPR fantasy points until Week 14. He did not have a single game with more than 2 targets with the team opting to play **Jeremy McNichols** over him in the pass-catching role. **Davante Adams** is an obvious regression candidate in 2026. His 23.3% touchdown rate and 14 touchdowns in 14 regular season games in 2025 are simply not replicable. He’s still an elite talent, but I refuse to chase those absurd touchdown numbers. Since 2020 Adams has not had back-to-back seasons with a touchdown rate over 10%. I’m avoiding him at his lofty draft cost.

**D.J. Moore** finished as the WR43 in PPR points per game in 2025, which is a clear regression from his previous production. The Bills have lacked a true WR1 since Stefon Diggs’ departure, consistently spreading the ball around without rhyme or reason. **Joe Brady’s** offense offers no guarantee of target share consistency. His fifth-round draft cost is too steep.

**Courtland Sutton** had a ceiling season in 2025, finishing as the WR16 in PPR points per game (13.6) with eight games of 16 or more fantasy points. With **Jaylen Waddle** now in the fold, a significant chunk of those targets disappears. New play-caller **Davis Webb** is also an unknown variable here. His offense may not suit Sutton’s game the way **Sean Payton’s** did. The round 7-8 range offers better value elsewhere.

**DK Metcalf** is going several rounds before **Michael Pittman Jr.** on almost every platform. This gap is difficult to justify when our projections have Pittman slightly ahead in PPR formats. In 2025, Metcalf had only four games with 16 or more PPR points. You are better off waiting a couple rounds and taking Pittman and using the round 7-8 pick on a higher upside receiver, quarterback, or tight end than selecting Metcalf this year.

The Cardinals led the NFL in pass attempts last season, it’s extremely unlikely that is the case again this season. A new coaching staff and the third overall pick spent on running back **Jeremiyah Love** signal a clear shift in offensive identity. **Michael Wilson’s** breakout context from last season is also being overlooked. Wilson averaged fewer than four points per game from Weeks 1 through 5 with Kyler Murray starting and a healthy Marvin Harrison Jr. on the field. He then averaged over 16 points per game the...

There’s just no way **Travis Hunter** will be a consistent starter you can trust unless there are multiple injuries to the Jaguars wide receiver room. He’s going as a top-100 pick right now on ESPN and top-150 on most platforms; there are much higher ceiling options available this late in drafts.

Doubs signed with the Patriots this offseason, but he will be a start/sit nightmare week-to-week competing for targets with **Kayshon Boutte, Demario Douglas, Mack Hollins, and Hunter Henry** behind A.J. Brown. Doubs will likely be in a role similar to **Stefon Diggs** last year where he is playing only around half the snaps. Don’t waste a later round pick on him.

While not being overly sought after in drafts, **Brandon Aiyuk’s** situation is giving very similar vibes to **Joe Mixon** from last season. The two situations are very different, but the outcome is looking increasingly likely to be the same. There’s a very real chance that Aiyuk doesn’t play a single snap this season. And if he does, are we sure Aiyuk is still a talented NFL WR?

While talented, **Tyler Warren** is too costly in drafts, especially when factoring in how closely he’s being taken to **Colston Loveland**. Warren doesn’t have the ceiling of Loveland, and our projections much prefer him in rounds 3-5 of drafts than Tyler Warren. **Daniel Jones** is coming back from a torn achilles, which brings more risk to the entire Colts passing attack. Warren’s draft cost is simply too high for this level of risk early in drafts.

**Harold Fannin Jr.** projects as a negative regression candidate in 2026. Subpar quarterback play and a new play-caller make a repeat of his rookie season an uphill battle. With Fannin going in the first 90 picks of most drafts, I’d rather take one of the big three TE options or wait a bit longer and take tight ends like **Tucker Kraft, George Kittle, Sam LaPorta, or Isaiah Likely** who have comparable (or better) ceilings later in drafts.

**Matthew Stafford** is coming off an MVP season with a ridiculously high 7.5% touchdown rate. Since 2020 Stafford has not had back-to-back seasons with a touchdown rate over 5%. Stafford has an inflated draft cost this year despite the likely negative regression that will hit him this season in the touchdown category. I’d much rather wait and take a quarterback with rushing upside later in my draft than waste a mid-round pick that is very unlikely to sustain league-leading touchdown efficiency again this season.

Nobody is actively looking to draft **Cam Ward** in redraft leagues, but I want to acknowledge just how terrible Ward was statistically as a rookie. He was 42nd in fantasy points per game among QBs, 34th in rushing yards per game, and 35th in passing TD rate. It is truly hard to be any worse than this statistically. They added some exciting weapons, and a much better play-caller in **Brian Daboll**, but I’d much rather take the quarterbacks available a few rounds earlier like **Malik Willis, Kyler Murray, and Tyler...

Corum is a league-winning handcuff if Kyren Williams misses time and he should offer a usable floor even without a Kyren injury. Off-season reporting from The Athletic suggests this backfield will be closer to a 50-50 split than current ADP suggests. Last year after the Rams Week 8 bye Corum regularly alternated drives and was playing ~40% of snaps compared to the 25% snap share he had before the bye.

Brooks enters 2026 healthy with a clear path to becoming the Panther’s lead back. Carolina let **Rico Dowdle** walk for a reason. Brooks has a very high ceiling if he stays healthy, and he’s going too late in drafts.

However, all signs this offseason point to Lloyd being fully healthy and in the clear lead for the Packers RB2 role behind **Josh Jacobs**. Last year as a rookie, Shough averaged 17.6 fantasy points per game across his 9 full games. He finished the season strong with six straight games over 17 fantasy points. We often see quarterbacks take a step forward in year 2, and he should benefit from the Saints fast-paced offense and the addition of talented rookie wide receiver **Jordyn Tyson**. Our projections have Shough ranked ahead of his ADP on every platform.

There is no hiding the fact that Kyler’s last season on the Cardinals was underwhelming. In his six games where he played over 50% of the snaps last season, **Ryan Flournoy** averaged 13.4 PPR points per game. Flournoy would be an instant WR3 with WR2 upside in fantasy football if CeeDee Lamb or George Pickens miss time, and he has the potential for usable weeks in deeper leagues without any injuries.

**Zachariah Branch** was one of our favorite rookies in this class, and his skill set pairs well with Drake London’s. Branch is going outside the top-200 picks, but profiles as the after-the-catch, dynamic slot receiver Kevin Stefanski likes to deploy. He is worth your final pick.

**Jalen Nailor** was one of the most underrated offseason signings for the Raiders. Nailor has experience with Kirk Cousins and Klint Kubiak, and his 15.2 yards per reception ranked 10th highest in the NFL last season despite the fact that over half his snaps came from the slot and he had one of the worst QB situations in the league. He has a real path to the most WR targets in Las Vegas.

He recorded three or more receptions in four of his final five games in 2025. If he becomes the top red zone target for **Malik Willis** (which is certainly possible), he would have a pathway to fantasy football excellence. He’s going undrafted in every league.

Hear me out on this one. I’m fully aware that **Kaleb Johnson** was horrendous as a rookie in his limited opportunities. But, he was a third round pick, and if Rico Dowdle or Jaylen Warren miss time, he would be thrust into a vital role in the Pittsburgh offense. Side note: He was one of my favorite prospects in his class, and I am still holding out hope.

All signs point to more two TE sets for the Raiders this season which should lead to usable fantasy weeks with Mayer.
